studies.title: Distracting yourself from something upsetting makes it hit harder the next time you see it
studies.ns_score_reason: clean EEG evidence that a popular coping tactic quietly stores up trouble; limited by lab pictures rather than real distress.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (0 news hits)
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Seventy-three participants did a working memory task while unpleasant and neutral images flashed up between trials, then saw the same images again in a surprise recognition test alongside brand-new ones. Keeping the mind busy reduced brain response (the late positive potential) to negative images at the time — but on the second encounter, those same images drew as much attention and were rated as arousing as pictures never seen before, unlike images viewed under low load. Images processed under high load were also recognized less accurately.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that "disengaged" regulation — loading up your attention so the upsetting thing doesn't land — works only in the moment and prevents the habituation that would otherwise blunt the stimulus later, echoing what is known about avoidance in anxiety treatment.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the very ordinary habit of scrolling or busying yourself through a distressing news clip. The surprise: your brain treats the picture as if you had never seen it when it returns, and you remember it worse. Call Annmarie MacNamara's lab at Texas A&M, which has run a series of these load-versus-emotion experiments.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health or workplace outlet on "productive avoidance" — why keeping busy after a shock is the most socially approved and least examined coping strategy, and how it interacts with exposure-based therapy logic.
studies.caveats: Standardized emotional pictures, not personally relevant distress; single session with an immediate second exposure, so nothing is known about days or weeks later; single-center undergraduate-style sample.

studies.title: Deliberately dampening your own good mood softens the crash that follows
studies.ns_score_reason: preregistered randomized experiment giving a rational motive to a habit usually framed as purely self-defeating.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In a preregistered randomized design, 102 community adults were put through a happiness induction, then randomly assigned to two minutes of dampening (talking down their good mood) or relaxation, before a sadness induction. The drop from high to low positive affect was significantly smaller in the dampening group — the first experimental evidence that dampening works as "emotional contrast avoidance," a mechanism previously proposed for worry.
studies.why_it_matters: Dampening positive emotion is treated as a transdiagnostic vulnerability for depression and bipolar disorder; showing it delivers a real short-term payoff explains why people keep doing it and reframes how clinicians might tackle it.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the person who refuses to celebrate good news in case it is snatched away — and the finding that they are, in one narrow sense, right: the fall really is shorter. Then the catch: the strategy that smooths the drop also flattens the peak. Filip Raes's group at KU Leuven, with Michelle Newman at Penn State (author of the contrast avoidance model), are the calls.
studies.wider_angle: A psychology-of-superstition piece for a general-interest magazine on "pre-emptive pessimism" — from touching wood to defensive pessimism in exam takers — and the growing evidence that these habits are functional emotion management rather than irrational tics.
studies.caveats: Unselected community sample, single laboratory session, lab-induced mood rather than life events, no follow-up on longer-term costs.

studies.title: In depression, reappraisal is barely used — and distraction only helps when you actually want to feel good
studies.ns_score_reason: undermines the therapy world's favorite strategy in daily life, though N is modest.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (2 news hits)
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Sixty-five clinically depressed adults completed seven days of experience sampling reporting their moment-to-moment emotion goals and which strategies they used. Reappraisal — the mainstay of cognitive therapy — was rarely chosen and showed no link to later mood. Wanting to reduce negative feeling predicted more use of acceptance, which did improve mood; distraction improved mood only when paired with a live goal to feel better, and made things worse when that goal was absent.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the effectiveness of a coping strategy depends on the motive behind it, not the strategy itself — a shift from "which technique works" to "what are you trying to achieve right now."
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is that the technique most people are taught in therapy and self-help apps almost never gets deployed spontaneously by depressed people in real life, and does nothing to mood when it is. Open on a person mid-week reaching for their phone: same act, opposite effect depending on intention. Call Ana Pacheco (Complutense University of Madrid) and Kristof Hoorelbeke at Ghent.
studies.wider_angle: For a digital health or tech outlet: mental health apps prescribe strategies but almost never ask what the user wants to feel — a piece on whether goal-sensitive "just-in-time" interventions are the next generation.
studies.caveats: N = 65, observational within-person design (cannot establish causation), self-reported strategy use, seven days only, no healthy comparison group.

studies.title: People will pay money to find out exactly how much a coming pain will hurt
studies.ns_score_reason: pushes back on the fashionable "information avoidance" story with real heat pain and real money; exploratory design tempers it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Participants played coin-flip lotteries in which each outcome delivered a different intensity of heat pain, and could bid small sums of money to learn the outcome before it arrived. Two-thirds bid regularly, and bids rose with both higher expected pain and greater uncertainty between the two possible intensities. Some of those who paid for the information reported feeling less pain when they knew what was coming, and bidding correlated with habitual use of expressive suppression.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the increasingly popular claim that people systematically avoid bad news, and hints that advance knowledge is itself a form of emotion regulation that changes the felt intensity of pain.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the medical version of the experiment — the patient asking the dentist to tell them exactly what is about to happen. The surprise is that when the bad thing is unavoidable, wanting to know is the majority position, and knowing may actually hurt less. Stefan Bode (NYU Abu Dhabi / University of Melbourne) is the call.
studies.wider_angle: For a medicine or health-policy outlet: what this means for how clinicians deliver warnings before painful procedures, and the long-running debate over "blunters versus monitors" in patient communication.
studies.caveats: Explicitly exploratory, no preregistration reported, a third of participants never bid, pain-reduction effect only in a subgroup, small monetary stakes may not scale to real decisions.

studies.title: Being properly listened to makes advice work better — and shows up as synchrony between two brains
studies.ns_score_reason: a familiar folk truth given hyperscanning evidence and a specific mechanism; all-female dyads limit reach.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Seventy-four female pairs were scanned simultaneously with functional near-infrared spectroscopy while one partner shared a negative experience and the other listened either actively or passively before trying to help — by reframing the situation (reappraisal) or by encouraging acceptance. Active listening reduced the sharer's negative emotion more, and did so especially when followed by reappraisal; brain-to-brain synchrony between the listener's frontal pole and the sharer's dorsolateral prefrontal cortex tracked this advantage.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives a testable account of why the same reframing advice lands differently depending on how the listener behaved beforehand — with implications for how support is trained in helplines, clinics and couples.
studies.pitch_angle: The pitch is that reframing someone's problem only works if you have earned it in the preceding minutes, and the earning is visible as two prefrontal cortices falling into step. Open on the friend who jumps straight to "look at it this way." Yuanmeng Wang's lab at East China Normal University.
studies.wider_angle: For a workplace or management outlet: what hyperscanning research is revealing about listening as a measurable skill, and whether "active listening" training in organizations has any evidence behind it.
studies.caveats: All-female dyads recruited in one country (population may not generalize), strangers in a laboratory task, fNIRS measures cortical surface only, synchrony is correlational.

studies.title: Couples who acknowledge each other mid-argument pull each other out of bad moods in real time
studies.ns_score_reason: second-by-second behavioral coding of real conflicts with a prospective outcome, but observational.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Ninety-three expectant couples had a 15-minute recorded conflict discussion during pregnancy, coded second by second for affect. Using state-space grids, the researchers showed that when one partner signaled validation — acknowledgment, interest, genuine understanding — the other was more likely to transition out of negative affect into neutral or positive states within the conversation. Frequent validators had better postpartum relationship quality, and men who validated more reported lower parenting stress.
studies.why_it_matters: It isolates a single, trainable behavior as the moment-to-moment mechanism of couple co-regulation, and links it to how well people weather the transition to parenthood.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell it on the granularity: not "communication matters" but a specific behavior whose effect on your partner's mood can be timed to the second, filmed while both partners were pregnant with their first child. Darby Saxbe's lab at USC is the call.
studies.wider_angle: A parenting-magazine or long-read feature on the new-father data emerging from Saxbe's cohort — the men who validate most report the least parenting stress — and why fathers' emotional labor is only now being measured.
studies.caveats: N = 93 couples, observational (cannot establish causation), single 15-minute lab conflict, self-reported postpartum outcomes, sample of expectant first-time parents may not generalize.

studies.title: Five weeks of slow breathing changes how the amygdala and prefrontal cortex covary in size
studies.ns_score_reason: large randomized biofeedback trial with a rare active-comparison design; structural covariance is an abstract outcome to explain.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (0 news hits)
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: In 151 adults (100 younger, 51 older), participants did five weeks of daily heart rate variability biofeedback aimed at either increasing (Osc+) or decreasing (Osc−) heart rate oscillations, with MRI before and after. The two conditions produced opposing patterns of structural covariance between the right amygdala and left medial prefrontal cortex; in the increase condition, volume changes in the left amygdala ran inversely to changes in the right orbitofrontal cortex.
studies.why_it_matters: It supports the idea that deliberately manipulating heart rhythms feeds back onto emotion-regulation circuitry rather than merely reflecting it — evidence for a bodily route into brain plasticity, though the clinical meaning is unproven.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the direction of travel: not brain to heart but heart to brain, in a randomized design where one group was asked to make their heart rhythms *less* variable. Open on the daily 20 minutes of paced breathing volunteers did at home. Mara Mather (USC / Max Planck Institute for Human Development) leads the trial.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist neuroscience or fitness-technology outlet: HRV has become a consumer metric on every wearable — a piece assessing what the trial evidence actually shows about training it, versus what the apps claim.
studies.caveats: Structural covariance is an indirect measure with contested interpretation; no passive control arm reported here; secondary analysis of an existing trial; behavioral or clinical benefit not tested in this paper.

studies.title: Four weeks of memory training changes how six-year-olds' brains handle upsetting images
studies.ns_score_reason: randomized, three-arm, with ERP outcomes in young children; effect appeared for only one of two training tasks.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Seventy-eight children aged six to seven were randomly assigned to one of two working memory training programs or a control group for 16–20 sessions over about four weeks, with EEG recorded before and after while they looked at emotional pictures and were told to focus on non-emotional details. Only the "animal span" training group showed a reduced late positive potential to negative pictures under those distraction instructions, with source estimates pointing to reduced prefrontal activation.
studies.why_it_matters: Working memory training has a poor record for producing transfer to anything useful; this is one of the more specific claims yet that it might transfer to emotion regulation, in a developmental window where those skills are forming.
studies.pitch_angle: Given how thoroughly brain training has been debunked for adults, the story is the narrow, task-specific exception in children — and the fact that the two training programs did not behave the same way. Open in a classroom. Renlai Zhou's group at Nanjing University.
studies.wider_angle: For an education outlet: the school-based cognitive-training industry, and what a neural marker with no behavioral outcome does and does not license anyone to sell to parents.
studies.caveats: N = 78 split three ways, single-center, brain outcome only — no evidence children regulated emotion better in daily life; effect emerged for one training task and not the other; no follow-up.

studies.title: Depressed patients get real, short-lived relief from telling someone — then the cycle restarts
studies.ns_score_reason: 4,711 momentary reports from diagnosed patients modeling a feedback loop, but self-report throughout.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Two hundred and five patients diagnosed with depression or anxiety disorders reported state depression, momentary attachment feelings and social regulation behavior three times daily for 10 days, producing 4,711 assessments analyzed with dynamic structural equation modeling. Feeling low predicted more social sharing at the next report — sometimes via a spike in attachment anxiety — and that sharing then predicted a genuine dip in depressed mood. But attachment anxiety and depression also reinforced each other, and both drove more emotional suppression next time.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows two loops running in parallel in the same people: one that helps and one that traps, with momentary insecurity determining which one you enter.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the paradox: the same low mood pushes people toward both the thing that helps (talking) and the thing that doesn't (bottling up), depending on how secure they happen to feel at that moment. Open on a patient's phone buzzing for the third time that day. Xinyi Zhou at Zhejiang University, with Martin Teicher at Harvard Medical School.
studies.wider_angle: For a mental health or sociology outlet: the "just talk to someone" message is everywhere — a piece on what intensive daily-life data reveal about who actually benefits from disclosure and who is made more anxious by it.
studies.caveats: Entirely self-reported, observational (within-person prospective associations, not causation), 10-day window, clinic sample in China may not generalize.

studies.title: Persistent grumpiness and explosive tempers look like different things in children's brains
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: first neural dissociation of two irritability components in young children; whole-brain interaction findings need replication.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: One hundred and sixty children (mean age 6.2) recruited with an irritability-enriched screening design did a reward task in an MRI scanner, with caregivers rating tonic irritability (chronic irritable mood) and phasic irritability (temper outbursts) separately. The two dimensions mapped onto partially separable frontostriatal and limbic patterns: tonic irritability was tied to altered ventral striatal connectivity when children missed out or failed, phasic irritability to sharper amygdala–prefrontal and striatal–cingulate distinctions between reward and no reward.
studies.why_it_matters: Irritability is one of the commonest reasons young children are referred to mental health services and is usually treated as one thing; the data suggest chronic irritable mood and reactive outbursts may need different explanations and different interventions.
studies.pitch_angle: Pitch it on the parental distinction everyone already makes intuitively — the child who is always a bit cross versus the child who erupts — and the evidence that these are not simply degrees of the same trait by age six. Lea Dougherty at Maryland and Jillian Wiggins at San Diego State.
studies.wider_angle: For a clinical or policy outlet: the fraught history of diagnosing childhood irritability, from the bipolar-diagnosis surge to disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, and whether dimensional neural evidence can settle it.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, caregiver-reported irritability, complex three-way interactions in whole-brain analyses are prone to false positives and await replication, community sample enriched for irritability.

studies.title: Social stress, not trauma, is what stops refugees leaning on other people to manage their feelings
studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and a genuinely unexpected direction for trauma exposure; cross-sectional.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Five hundred and sixty-one refugees in Australia reported trauma exposure, post-migration social and practical stressors, use of other people to regulate their emotions, and symptoms of PTSD, depression and anger. Social stressors — isolation, discrimination, loss of community — predicted higher depression through reduced use of every interpersonal regulation strategy. Trauma exposure went the other way: more trauma was associated with *lower* depression via *greater* use of these strategies.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts attention from what happened before flight to what happens after arrival, identifying social conditions in the host country as the thing that severs people from their main emotional resource.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that trauma exposure did not sever people from social support — social stress in the resettlement country did. Open on the practical detail of an isolated resettlement placement. Angela Nickerson and Belinda Liddell (UNSW Sydney) are the calls, with the Australian Red Cross as a partner.
studies.wider_angle: For a policy or international-affairs outlet: resettlement design as mental health intervention — how housing dispersal and community placement decisions may matter as much as trauma-focused therapy provision.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and self-reported (cannot establish causation or direction), single host country, refugees recruited through service organizations may not represent those outside the system.

studies.title: How well you read your own body — not how you think about feelings — separates the active from the inactive
studies.ns_score_reason: a null on the fashionable variable in a sample of over 1,000; observational.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (1 news hits)
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In 1,073 adults (mean age 35), cognitive emotion regulation strategies did not distinguish inactive, moderately active and highly active people once age, sex, education and BMI were controlled. Interoceptive sensibility did: active groups were more attuned to bodily signals, while inactive people reported more anxiety, more depression and more attention to uncomfortable sensations. Attitudes toward physical effort differed across all three activity levels and were predicted mainly by interoceptive variables — low worry about bodily sensations predicted approach; listening closely without being able to distract predicted avoidance. Moderate and highly active groups did not differ from one another.
studies.why_it_matters: It points away from "regulate your thoughts to get moving" and toward the sensory relationship people have with their own bodies — and suggests moderate activity may capture most of the psychological benefit.
studies.pitch_angle: Two hooks: mindset variables did nothing, and the highly active group was psychologically indistinguishable from the merely moderately active. Open on someone deciding whether the burn in their legs is information or a threat. Alice Bodart at the University of Mons.
studies.wider_angle: For a fitness or health outlet: interoception as the missing variable in exercise adherence, and why programs that teach people to interpret discomfort may outperform motivational messaging.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and self-reported throughout, including activity levels (IPAQ is known to over-report), no causal direction, volunteer online sample.

studies.title: Fathers are slower than mothers to respond to a distressed baby — and three-way play stresses infants most
studies.ns_score_reason: moment-by-moment physiological co-regulation across mother, father and triad, rarely done; effects are small-scale and correlational.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Eighty families with three-month-old infants completed successive two-minute free-play sessions — mother–infant, father–infant, and all three together — with parental intrusive or withdrawn behavior coded in five-second intervals against the infant's averaged heart rate. Intrusive and withdrawn parenting predicted subsequent rises in infant heart rate; for intrusiveness the relationship was bidirectional, indicating genuine back-and-forth co-regulation. Fathers responded to infant arousal with a delay, and triadic play was associated with both stronger couplings and higher infant heart rate overall.
studies.why_it_matters: It captures co-regulation as it actually happens — in seconds, not sessions — and shows the family unit, not just the mother–infant dyad, shapes an infant's physiological state.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive detail is that both parents together was the most physiologically demanding configuration for a three-month-old. Open on a family in the lab's playroom, the video timestamped in five-second slices. Hervé Tissot at Lausanne's Center for Family Studies.
studies.wider_angle: For a parenting or science-and-society outlet: the quiet expansion of infant research beyond mothers, and what a decade of father data has done to attachment theory's assumptions.
studies.caveats: N = 80 families, brief two-minute observations, fixed session order not counterbalanced as described, heart rate is a coarse index of arousal, observational.

studies.title: People with functional neurological disorder say they struggle to manage emotions — the lab does not show it
studies.ns_score_reason: a preregistered multimethod null that complicates a dominant clinical narrative; underpowered lab subsample.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (0 news hits)
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In a preregistered study, 109 people with functional neurological disorder and 88 controls completed questionnaires, and a subsample (33 versus 33) did laboratory tasks measuring which regulation strategy they chose and how well it worked, indexed by subjective arousal and startle reflex. On questionnaires, the FND group reported far more difficulty, more alexithymia, more childhood trauma and less use of other people to regulate. In the lab, groups did not differ in what they chose or how well it worked. Notably, having someone else help reframe a situation produced lower startle responses than doing it alone, in both groups.
studies.why_it_matters: It cautions against reading self-reported emotion regulation deficits as evidence of a real-time regulatory failure — and highlights interpersonal regulation as the more promising place to look in FND.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the gap between what patients report about themselves and what can be measured when they are doing it — a live issue for a condition whose psychological framing patients often contest. The finding that a second person's reframing calms the startle reflex more than your own is the vivid detail. Inga Niedtfeld's group (Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim).
studies.wider_angle: For a medical or long-read outlet: functional neurological disorder's contested status, and how the field is trying to build objective measures for a diagnosis historically defined by their absence.
studies.caveats: Lab subsample of 33 per group is underpowered for interactions — the authors say so; null results cannot be taken as evidence of no difference; self-report and lab measures were not matched constructs; needs replication.

studies.title: Whether you cry in front of someone depends on how agreeable you are — and on whose sadness it is
studies.ns_score_reason: highly relatable and a nice reversal of what you would predict about agreeable people; questionnaire-based and culturally specific.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: One hundred and sixty-nine Japanese university students reported crying experiences across six everyday categories, alongside empathy and personality measures. People scoring higher on agreeableness were more likely to suppress tears in front of others specifically when crying was triggered by a close person's sadness — apparently to avoid burdening that person — while showing no such suppression in other crying contexts.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes crying as a socially calibrated act rather than an overflow of feeling, with the calibration depending on both personality and who is upset.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive turn: the warmest, most agreeable people are the ones most likely to hold back tears at a friend's bad news, because crying would make it about them. Open at a hospital bedside or a funeral. Kei Miyashiro at Utsunomiya University.
studies.wider_angle: For a culture or anthropology outlet: crying norms across societies, and why almost all the psychology of tears has been built on Western samples — Japan being one of the low-crying-frequency outliers.
studies.caveats: Retrospective self-report, single university sample in one country (population may not generalize), cross-sectional, no measurement of actual crying behavior.

studies.title: Mothers who bottle up their feelings have toddlers with more screen time
studies.ns_score_reason: a specific, relatable link with a clean strategy dissociation; entirely cross-sectional self-report.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (0 news hits)
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Two hundred and ninety-six mothers of toddlers aged 18–36 months reported their habitual emotion regulation strategies and both their own and their child's screen use, separated into interactive and non-interactive forms. Higher expressive suppression was associated with more of the mother's own passive screen use and with both types of toddler screen use; cognitive reappraisal showed no association with anything. Mothers' passive screen use was in turn linked to more toddler screen use of both kinds.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests family screen habits may track how parents handle their own emotions rather than their beliefs about screens — a different target for guidance, if the direction of causation holds up.
studies.pitch_angle: Frame it around the parenting-advice gap: guidance targets screen-time rules, but the variable that predicted toddler screen use here was whether the mother suppresses her feelings. Be explicit that this is correlational. Koeun Choi at Virginia Tech.
studies.wider_angle: For a family or technology outlet: the emerging evidence that parental screen use predicts children's better than any rule does, and what that means for "digital parenting" advice built around limits.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and entirely maternal self-report (cannot establish causation, and suppression may bias reporting), mothers only, online convenience sample, no direct measurement of screen use.

studies.title: Savoring works just as well on the biggest highs as on the small ones
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean Bayesian null that corrects an assumption imported from the negative-emotion literature; narrow.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (0 news hits)
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Ninety participants were asked either to savor or simply to view high- and low-arousing positive images while EEG and ratings were collected. Savoring boosted the late positive potential and both arousal and valence ratings for both intensities, and Bayesian analysis supported the absence of any interaction — with weak hints that savoring works slightly *better* on high-arousal material.
studies.why_it_matters: Down-regulating negative emotion by engaging with content fails when the content is intensely arousing; this shows the reverse does not apply to positive emotion, so savoring need not be reserved for small pleasures.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the symmetry that isn't: strategies for turning feelings down and turning them up obey different rules. The practical takeaway — savoring the big moments works — is unusually easy to picture. Annmarie MacNamara's lab at Texas A&M.
studies.wider_angle: For a wellbeing or psychology-of-happiness feature: savoring has quietly become the best-evidenced positive-psychology technique while gratitude journaling gets the headlines; a piece on what the lab evidence actually supports.
studies.caveats: N = 90, single lab session, standardized images rather than personal experiences, no clinical sample, effects on ratings partly anecdotal in Bayesian terms.

studies.title: We rarely use one coping strategy at a time — and only two combinations actually lower distress
studies.ns_score_reason: brings a realistic "strategy stacking" framing to emotion regulation; student sample, self-report.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: One hundred and six university students completed seven days of experience sampling, bracketed by lab sessions measuring heart rate variability and cognitive control, reporting how many strategies they used per emotional event. More intense events prompted more strategies at once; people with greater emotion dysregulation used more strategies but had more negative affect. Within bouts of multi-strategy regulation, only situation selection (removing yourself) and reinterpretation predicted lower daily negative affect.
studies.why_it_matters: Almost all emotion regulation research tests one strategy at a time, which is not how people behave; this points to combinations rather than single techniques as the useful unit of analysis.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is quantity versus quality — people who struggle most throw the most strategies at a problem and feel worse. Open on someone cycling through four coping tactics in ten minutes after a difficult message. Bryan Denny at Rice University.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychology outlet: the "polyregulation" turn, and how it exposes the artificiality of a generation of single-strategy laboratory experiments.
studies.caveats: N = 106 undergraduates (population may not generalize), self-reported strategies and affect, observational, seven days.

studies.title: Sensory sensitivity, not IQ, predicts whether self-injury in autistic children gets better or worse
studies.ns_score_reason: large longitudinal autism cohort addressing a serious, under-covered outcome; observational.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers assessed self-injurious behavior in 325 autistic children aged 2–5 and 161 aged 4–9, with 122 followed at both time points. Around three-quarters had some level of self-injury early on; only 9% had none at either point. Severity moved substantially between categories over time, and improvement in sensory features and higher later IQ raised the odds of severity decreasing — while baseline severity was the only predictor of getting worse.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes self-injury as a fluctuating behavior tied to sensory experience and dysregulation rather than a fixed feature of intellectual disability, and identifies sensory responsivity as a candidate lever.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the prevalence figure — nearly all these preschoolers showed some self-injury at some point — and the finding that children whose sensory sensitivities eased were the ones whose self-injury eased too. Christine Wu Nordahl at the UC Davis MIND Institute.
studies.wider_angle: For a disability or health outlet: self-injury is one of the most distressing and least discussed aspects of autism for families, and sensory-based interventions have a thin evidence base — a piece on what parents are currently offered.
studies.caveats: Observational (correlated change, not causation), attrition between time points, sensory features and dysregulation both parent-reported, single research site.

studies.title: Sixteen hours of home audio reveals which mothers snap when a child gets very upset
studies.ns_score_reason: striking naturalistic method and a clean diathesis-stress interaction; very small sample.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Fifty-three families with a child aged 3–5 wore recorders capturing 16 hours of home audio, from which four to ten emotional episodes per child were coded for the child's intensity and the mother's response, with language analyzed for emotion words. Rising child distress predicted more unsupportive responses and less positive emotion talk in real time — but only among mothers who reported a trait tendency to become distressed by their child's emotions, and this held even after accounting for general emotion regulation difficulties.
studies.why_it_matters: It separates a parenting-specific vulnerability from general emotional difficulty, and shows it only manifests when the situation is intense enough — a textbook diathesis-stress pattern captured in the kitchen rather than the lab.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the method: researchers listening to 16 hours of ordinary family life to find the moments where things tip. And the finding that "how well you regulate emotions" in general does not predict how you respond to your own crying child. Niyantri Ravindran at the University of Georgia.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology-and-ethics or social-science outlet: naturalistic home audio recording is transforming developmental research — a piece on what these devices are capturing and what consent and privacy look like when the data is a family's daily life.
studies.caveats: N = 53 families, mothers only, self-reported trait distress reactivity, observational, one day of recording per family, single-site US sample.

studies.title: Virtual reality meditation shifts children's heart rhythms in four short sessions
studies.ns_score_reason: timely and relatable school application with a physiological outcome, but no control group.

studies.the_study: One hundred and twenty-seven children aged 9–12 completed four virtual reality mindfulness sessions with heart rate variability measured throughout and emotional skills assessed before and after. High-frequency power and physiological coherence rose, indicating greater parasympathetic activity, and children reported improved emotional clarity and ability to repair their moods. Year 5 children gained more in heart rate variability than their older peers.
studies.why_it_matters: Getting children to sit still and meditate is the main obstacle to school mindfulness programs; the finding that headsets produce measurable autonomic shifts in four sessions is worth following, though without a comparison group the effect could be practice, novelty or expectation.
studies.pitch_angle: Open in the classroom, with a row of nine-year-olds in headsets. The honest frame: physiological change is a step beyond the questionnaire outcomes school mindfulness usually reports, but this needs a controlled trial. Amaiur Olarza at the University of the Basque Country.
studies.wider_angle: For an education or technology outlet: VR is arriving in schools mostly through wellbeing programs rather than teaching, with almost no regulatory scrutiny of headset use in under-13s.
studies.caveats: No control group, short intervention with no follow-up, low-frequency HRV interpretation contested (authors acknowledge), self-reported emotional skills, single region.

studies.journal: Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy

studies.the_study: Researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with 29 men in community-based treatment for emotion regulation difficulties and violence in intimate or family settings, then thematically analyzed how they understood sexual consent within relationships. Three positions emerged — consent as fundamental, consent as already given by virtue of commitment, and consent as a burden — which the authors describe as an "elasticity" that, stretched far enough, breaks into non-consensual contact.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents in participants' own words how consent norms erode inside long-term relationships, in the group where that erosion has the highest stakes — useful for designing intervention content, if not for estimating prevalence.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is access: these are men currently in treatment for intimate partner violence explaining, unprompted, why they think consent works differently after a certain number of years together. Élodie Garant and Tamsin Higgs at the University of Montréal.
studies.wider_angle: For a social-affairs or legal outlet: how criminal law and public campaigns handle consent within marriage and long relationships, and the gap between the post-#MeToo public conversation and what happens behind closed doors.
studies.caveats: Qualitative, N = 29, a treatment-seeking sample selected for violence (population does not generalize to men in general), interview accounts are self-presented, single city.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Cognitive reappraisal — the flagship skill of cognitive therapy and of nearly every mental health app — keeps coming up empty in this batch, while regulation that runs through other people or through the body keeps coming up positive. Depressed adults almost never reach for reappraisal in daily life and it does nothing to their mood when they do (PMID 42660575); it was unrelated to mothers' and toddlers' screen habits (42447742) and failed to separate active from inactive people, where interoceptive sensibility did (42413746); polyregulation data found only situation selection and reinterpretation lowered daily negative affect (41806361). Meanwhile, having a second person reframe a situation cut startle reactivity more than doing it yourself, in patients and controls alike (42704885), active listening made subsequent reappraisal land better and showed up as brain-to-brain synchrony (42288208), mid-argument validation pulled partners out of negative affect in seconds (42441643), and five weeks of heart rate variability biofeedback reshaped amygdala–prefrontal structural covariance (42669395).

**Why pitch this now:** Reappraisal is the strategy being scaled fastest — into CBT apps, workplace resilience programs and school curricula — at exactly the moment that experience-sampling, dyadic and physiological studies are showing it is rarely used spontaneously, weakly tied to mood, and outperformed by acceptance, walking away, being listened to, and paced breathing.

**Angle:** A feature on the quiet demotion of "think about it differently" and the field's shift toward emotion regulation as a two-person, whole-body process — written for readers who have been handed a thought-record worksheet, and framed around what researchers now think the useful unit of analysis is: the pair, the situation and the nervous system rather than the lone mind.

**Potential headlines:**
- The coping skill therapy leans on hardest is the one people almost never use
- Reframing your problem works better when somebody else does it for you
- Talking yourself out of a bad mood is the hard way to do it

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Mind** — the section already runs single-strategy emotion regulation news; this is the synthesis piece those items keep gesturing at.
- **The Atlantic (Health)** — has an appetite for careful "the therapy consensus is shifting" pieces aimed at readers who have done CBT themselves.
- **The Guardian science desk** — strong readership interest in mental health app claims and the evidence gap behind resilience training.
- **Knowable Magazine** — well suited to a field-level review of how emotion regulation research moved from the solo lab task to dyads, wearables and daily-life sampling.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Emotion Regulation — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-08 | **Studies reviewed:** 22
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

### Study 1: Distracting yourself from something upsetting makes it hit harder the next time you see it
**PMID:** 42693580 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Recognition-accuracy result narrowed to negative pictures** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Images processed under high load were also recognized less accurately."
- **Abstract says:** "Negative pictures that had previously been presented on high-load compared to low-load trials also had lower recognition accuracy."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the recognition deficit for negative pictures specifically, relative to low-load negatives — not for images in general.
- **Suggested fix:** "Negative images seen under high load were also recognized less accurately than those seen under low load."

**Issue B. Habituation mechanism stated more firmly than the abstract does** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "works only in the moment and prevents the habituation that would otherwise blunt the stimulus later"
- **Abstract says:** "results suggest a mechanism through which disengaged emotion regulation strategies may fail to attenuate and may even increase emotional responses to stimuli when encountered again outside of the initial regulation context"
- **Problem:** "Prevents habituation" asserts a mechanism the authors only propose; the data show equivalence to novel pictures, not a demonstrated blocking of habituation.
- **Suggested fix:** "works only in the moment and may prevent the habituation that would otherwise blunt the stimulus later"

**Issue C. Late positive potential named as the index** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "reduced brain response (the late positive potential) to negative images at the time"
- **Abstract says:** "working memory load reduced picture processing" / "Electrocortical Processing" (title); the LPP is not named.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — plausible for this lab, but the specific ERP component is not stated.
- **Suggested fix:** "reduced the electrocortical response to negative images at the time (confirm the ERP component in the methods)"

*NS fit note:* 7/10 is defensible for a within-subject experimental EEG design with N = 73, though 6 would also be fair given the standardized-picture paradigm.

---

### Study 2: Deliberately dampening your own good mood softens the crash that follows
**PMID:** 42468402 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Flattens the peak" is not reported in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Then the catch: the strategy that smooths the drop also flattens the peak."
- **Abstract says:** "the negative emotional contrast from before versus after the sadness induction was less pronounced in the dampening condition compared to the relaxation condition."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports only the reduced contrast; it does not report that dampening lowered peak positive affect. Unverifiable from abstract only, and it is presented as a study finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "Then the likely catch — smoothing the drop plausibly means starting from a lower high, which the paper should be checked on before the pitch leans on it."

*Note (not an issue):* Michelle Newman is a co-author on this paper (Penn State), so the pitch should describe her as an author rather than an independent outside voice.

---

### Study 3: In depression, reappraisal is barely used — and distraction only helps when you actually want to feel good
**PMID:** 42660575 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. NS fit score high for a small self-report ESM study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — undermines the therapy world's favorite strategy in daily life, though N is modest."
- **Abstract says:** "a 7-day experience-sampling design in a sample of clinically depressed individuals (N = 65)"; "Lagged multilevel models"; authors call for future studies of "a wider array of emotion goals."
- **Problem:** A 7 rests on N = 65, entirely self-reported strategy and affect data, no comparison group, and a within-person observational design. The claim being sold ("reappraisal doesn't work in real life") is large relative to the evidence.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — undermines the therapy world's favourite strategy in daily life, but N = 65 and all measures are self-reported."

Study facts, statistics and direction of effect are otherwise accurately reproduced (reappraisal infrequent and unrelated to later affect; NA-reduction goal → acceptance → improved affect; distraction helpful only with a concurrent goal to increase PA, opposite pattern without it).

---

### Study 4: People will pay money to find out exactly how much a coming pain will hurt
**PMID:** 41347565 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Never bid" overstates the non-bidding third** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a third of participants never bid"
- **Abstract says:** "Two thirds of the sample regularly made bids."
- **Problem:** The remaining third did not bid *regularly*; the abstract does not say they never bid at all.
- **Suggested fix:** "a third of participants did not bid regularly"

**Issue B. NS fit score for an explicitly exploratory study with no N reported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — pushes back on the fashionable 'information avoidance' story with real heat pain and real money; exploratory design tempers it."
- **Abstract says:** "This exploratory study tested whether participants actively seek information…"; no sample size is given, and the pain-reduction result applies to "Some participants."
- **Problem:** A 7 rests on an exploratory design with an unreported N and a subgroup-only pain effect.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — pushes back on the fashionable 'information avoidance' story with real heat pain and real money, but the design is explicitly exploratory and the sample size is not stated in the abstract."

*Minor wording note:* the abstract says "suppression as an emotion regulation strategy"; the digest's "expressive suppression" adds a qualifier the abstract does not use.

---

### Study 5: Being properly listened to makes advice work better — and shows up as synchrony between two brains
**PMID:** 42288208 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Strangers" not stated in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "strangers in a laboratory task"
- **Abstract says:** "Seventy-four female dyads (the regulator and the target) were recruited to complete the IER task."
- **Problem:** The relationship between dyad members is not specified. Unverifiable from abstract only — and it matters, since acquaintance dyads would change the interpretation of the listening manipulation.
- **Suggested fix:** "laboratory dyads (check whether partners were strangers or acquainted)"

N (74 female dyads), the fNIRS hyperscanning design, the behavioural advantage of active listening for reappraisal, and the frontal pole–dlPFC synchrony pattern are all accurately reproduced.

---

### Study 6: Couples who acknowledge each other mid-argument pull each other out of bad moods in real time
**PMID:** 42441643 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Isolates the mechanism" overstates an observational finding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It isolates a single, trainable behavior as the moment-to-moment mechanism of couple co-regulation"
- **Abstract says:** "These findings underscore the importance of partner validation as a potential behavioral mechanism of interpersonal emotion regulation (i.e., coregulation), suggesting that it may facilitate better adjustment to parenthood."
- **Problem:** The authors call validation a *potential* mechanism; the digest presents it as identified and established, and adds "trainable," which was not tested. This also contradicts the digest's own caveat that the design is observational.
- **Suggested fix:** "It points to a single, specific behaviour as a potential moment-to-moment mechanism of couple co-regulation"

**Issue B. Temporal resolution ("second by second", "timed to the second")** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "coded second by second for affect" / "a specific behavior whose effect on your partner's mood can be timed to the second"
- **Abstract says:** "video recorded and coded for affective behaviors using the Specific Affect Coding System. Using state-space grids and grid-sequence analysis, we tracked real-time affective exchanges."
- **Problem:** The coding resolution is not stated. Unverifiable from abstract only; "timed to the second" also implies a causal precision the design does not deliver.
- **Suggested fix:** "coded continuously for affective behaviour" / "a specific behaviour whose association with the partner's next affective state can be tracked in real time"

**Issue C. "First child" not stated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "filmed while both partners were pregnant with their first child"
- **Abstract says:** "93 expectant-parent couples"; "The transition to parenthood represents a critical period."
- **Problem:** First-time parenthood is implied by the framing but not stated. Unverifiable from abstract only. (The phrasing "both partners were pregnant" is also loose.)
- **Suggested fix:** "filmed during the pregnancy, before the couple became parents"

---

### Study 7: Five weeks of slow breathing changes how the amygdala and prefrontal cortex covary in size
**PMID:** 42669395 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Randomized" not stated in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "large randomized biofeedback trial with a rare active-comparison design" / "in a randomized design where one group was asked to make their heart rhythms *less* variable"
- **Abstract says:** "Baseline and post-intervention MRI scans were collected from 151 participants (100 younger and 51 older adults) who completed 5 weeks of daily biofeedback sessions to either increase (Osc + condition) or decrease (Osc- condition) HRV."
- **Problem:** Random assignment is not mentioned. Unverifiable from abstract only (the parent trial may well be randomized, but it should be confirmed before the word is used in a pitch).
- **Suggested fix:** "large biofeedback trial with a rare active-comparison design (confirm random assignment in the parent trial)"

**Issue B. "Daily 20 minutes of paced breathing" not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on the daily 20 minutes of paced breathing volunteers did at home."
- **Abstract says:** "5 weeks of daily biofeedback sessions"; no session duration or breathing protocol is given, and the Osc− arm is not described as slow breathing.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; also note the headline's "slow breathing" describes the Osc+ arm, not both conditions.
- **Suggested fix:** "Open on the daily home biofeedback sessions volunteers completed for five weeks."

The structural covariance results (right amygdala–left mPFC opposing patterns; left amygdala–right OFC inverse association in Osc+) are accurately reproduced, and the "clinical meaning is unproven" hedge is appropriate.

---

### Study 8: Four weeks of memory training changes how six-year-olds' brains handle upsetting images
**PMID:** 42632448 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Source localization presented without its "exploratory" label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "with source estimates pointing to reduced prefrontal activation"
- **Abstract says:** "Exploratory source localization further suggested reduced estimated activation in prefrontal-related regions."
- **Problem:** The abstract flags this analysis as exploratory and the activations as estimated; the digest presents it as a supporting result on equal footing with the LPP finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "with exploratory source estimates tentatively pointing to reduced prefrontal activation"

N (78), the three-arm randomized design, 16–20 sessions over ~four weeks, and the single-group LPP effect are all accurate, and the caveats correctly note the absence of behavioural outcomes.

---

### Study 9: Depressed patients get real, short-lived relief from telling someone — then the cycle restarts
**PMID:** 41885910 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline narrows the sample to depression** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Depressed patients get real, short-lived relief from telling someone"
- **Abstract says:** "Participants (N = 205; Mage = 31.87…) with depression or anxiety disorders"
- **Problem:** The sample is mixed depression/anxiety patients; the body text says so but the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Patients with depression or anxiety get real, short-lived relief from telling someone"

**Issue B. Causal verb for a within-person association** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and both drove more emotional suppression next time"
- **Abstract says:** "Both were associated with increased expressive suppression at the subsequent measurement."
- **Problem:** "Drove" implies causation; the abstract calls the whole set of findings "preliminary evidence" for cyclical patterns. The caveats note this, but the body language contradicts them.
- **Suggested fix:** "and both were followed by more emotional suppression at the next report"

---

### Study 10: Persistent grumpiness and explosive tempers look like different things in children's brains
**PMID:** 42702353 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Referral-rate claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Irritability is one of the commonest reasons young children are referred to mental health services"
- **Abstract says:** "Irritability is a common and impairing feature of childhood psychopathology"
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; the specific referral claim needs an external citation before it appears in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Irritability is a common and impairing feature of childhood psychopathology"

Sample (160 children, mean age 6.17, irritability-enriched community screening), the tonic/phasic distinction, and the two independent effects (tonic → ventral striatal connectivity during nonreward/failure; phasic → amygdala–prefrontal and striatal–cingulate differentiation) are accurately reported, and "partially separable" matches "partially dissociable."

---

### Study 11: Social stress, not trauma, is what stops refugees leaning on other people to manage their feelings
**PMID:** 42619365 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal framing on a cross-sectional survey** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Social stress, not trauma, is what stops refugees leaning on other people to manage their feelings" / "identifying social conditions in the host country as the thing that severs people from their main emotional resource"
- **Abstract says:** "A sample of 561 refugees in Australia completed a survey…"; "Higher social stress was associated with elevated depression through reduced engagement of all interpersonal ER strategies"; "social stressors may be particularly harmful for refugee mental health and may be an important target mechanism."
- **Problem:** Both the headline ("is what stops") and the "Why it matters" line assert causation and direction from a single-timepoint self-report survey with SEM-estimated indirect paths. The caveats acknowledge this, but the body text contradicts them.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Social stress, not trauma, tracks with refugees turning away from other people to manage their feelings." Why it matters: "…pointing to social conditions in the host country as a candidate target, if the direction of effect holds up."

**Issue B. Specific stressor examples not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Social stressors — isolation, discrimination, loss of community —"
- **Abstract says:** "social and practical post-migration stressors"
- **Problem:** The content of the social stressor factor is not itemised in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Social stressors (as measured by a post-migration stressor scale)"

---

### Study 12: How well you read your own body — not how you think about feelings — separates the active from the inactive
**PMID:** 42413746 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Psychologically indistinguishable" contradicts the attitudes result** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the highly active group was psychologically indistinguishable from the merely moderately active"
- **Abstract says:** "No differences emerged between the Moderate and High groups in emotional regulation or interoception. Approach and Avoidance toward physical effort significantly differed across all three physical activity levels."
- **Problem:** The Moderate/High null applies only to emotion regulation and interoception; the two groups *did* differ on attitudes toward physical effort, which is one of the study's main outcomes. The pitch hook as written is not supported. (The digest's own body text notes attitudes differed across all three levels, so the pitch angle contradicts the study description.)
- **Suggested fix:** "the highly active group looked no different from the merely moderately active on emotion regulation and interoception — though their attitudes toward physical effort still differed"

Everything else checks out: N = 1,073, mean age 35.4, ANCOVAs controlling gender, age, education and BMI, the interoception and anxiety/depression pattern, the Approach/Avoidance predictors, and the "moderate levels may be sufficient" conclusion.

---

### Study 13: Fathers are slower than mothers to respond to a distressed baby — and three-way play stresses infants most
**PMID:** 42269373 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Heart rate read as "distress" and "stress"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Fathers are slower than mothers to respond to a distressed baby — and three-way play stresses infants most"
- **Abstract says:** "fathers showed delayed responses to infant arousal, whereas triadic interactions elicited stronger associations and higher HR levels"
- **Problem:** The measured variable is infant heart rate/arousal, not distress; higher HR in triadic free play could reflect engagement or excitement. The caveats note HR is a coarse index, but the headline goes further than the abstract's language.
- **Suggested fix:** "Fathers are slower than mothers to respond to a baby's arousal — and three-way play raises infant heart rate most"

**Issue B. Counterbalancing claim not verifiable** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "fixed session order not counterbalanced as described"
- **Abstract says:** "Eighty families with three-month-old infants completed three successive two-minute free-play sessions corresponding to these contexts."
- **Problem:** The abstract says the sessions were successive but does not state the order or whether it was counterbalanced. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "session order and whether it was counterbalanced is not specified in the abstract — check the methods"

---

### Study 14: People with functional neurological disorder say they struggle to manage emotions — the lab does not show it
**PMID:** 42704885 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Institutional attribution not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Inga Niedtfeld's group (Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim)."
- **Abstract says:** "Niedtfeld I, Hepp J, Schellhaas S, Steffen-Klatt A, Klaasen van Husen D, Held V." — no affiliations are listed.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** Verify the affiliation from the paper before naming it in the pitch.

**Issue B. The lab null is stated more flatly than the abstract does** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "In the lab, groups did not differ in what they chose or how well it worked."
- **Abstract says:** "no significant group differences in intrapersonal ER choice or success emerged… individuals with FND showed a non-significant trend toward reduced preference for interpersonal regulation… Across paradigms, ER success did not significantly differ between groups."
- **Problem:** The abstract flags a non-significant trend toward reduced preference for interpersonal regulation in FND — directionally consistent with the questionnaire data and relevant to the pitch's own "interpersonal regulation is the promising place to look" line.
- **Suggested fix:** "In the lab, groups did not differ significantly in what they chose or how well it worked, though FND participants showed a non-significant trend toward preferring interpersonal regulation less."

---

### Study 15: Whether you cry in front of someone depends on how agreeable you are — and on whose sadness it is
**PMID:** 42537321 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Null result in other crying contexts asserted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "while showing no such suppression in other crying contexts"
- **Abstract says:** "Japanese young adults with higher agreeableness scores tend to suppress crying in the presence of others in situations involving empathic responses to others' distress, specifically when crying was triggered by a close person's sadness."
- **Problem:** "Specifically when" implies context-dependence, but the abstract does not report explicit null findings for the other five categories. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "with the effect specific to that context in the reported analyses"

N (169), the Japanese university sample, the six crying categories, and the empathy/personality measures are accurate, and the caveats correctly flag retrospective self-report and single-country sampling.

---

### Study 16: Mothers who bottle up their feelings have toddlers with more screen time
**PMID:** 42447742 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Wider-angle claim goes beyond this study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the emerging evidence that parental screen use predicts children's better than any rule does"
- **Abstract says:** "Higher levels of maternal non-interactive screen media use were linked to greater non-interactive and interactive screen media use among toddlers."
- **Problem:** This study measured no screen-time rules, so it cannot support a comparison between parental modelling and rule-setting. Unverifiable from abstract only; needs external sourcing or rewording.
- **Suggested fix:** "the evidence that parental screen use tracks children's — and what that means for 'digital parenting' advice built around limits"

The core findings are correctly reproduced: N = 296 mothers of 18–36-month-olds, suppression linked to maternal non-interactive use and both forms of toddler use, no reappraisal associations, maternal non-interactive use linked to both forms of toddler use. The pitch's explicit "this is correlational" instruction is good practice.

---

### Study 17: Savoring works just as well on the biggest highs as on the small ones
**PMID:** 42398883 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Absence of any interaction" overstates the Bayesian result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Bayesian analysis supported the absence of any interaction — with weak hints that savoring works slightly *better* on high-arousal material"
- **Abstract says:** "Bayesian results were consistent with the absence of an interaction between stimulus arousal level and condition for the LPP, but yielded anecdotal evidence that savoring might be more effective at increasing arousal ratings of high- versus low-arousing pictures."
- **Problem:** The null-interaction evidence applies to the LPP specifically; for arousal ratings there was anecdotal evidence *of* an interaction. "Any interaction" is too broad.
- **Suggested fix:** "Bayesian analysis supported the absence of an interaction for the LPP, with anecdotal evidence of one in the opposite direction for arousal ratings — savouring may work slightly better on high-arousal material."

**Issue B. "Fails" overstates the down-regulation literature** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Down-regulating negative emotion by engaging with content fails when the content is intensely arousing"
- **Abstract says:** "engaged emotion regulation strategies… have been found to be better suited to low-arousing stimuli"
- **Problem:** "Better suited to low-arousing stimuli" is not the same as failing at high arousal.
- **Suggested fix:** "Engaged strategies for down-regulating negative emotion work better on low-arousing content"

---

### Study 18: We rarely use one coping strategy at a time — and only two combinations actually lower distress
**PMID:** 41806361 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Direction of the dysregulation–strategy-use finding is reversed** — Severity: Major

- **As written:** "people with greater emotion dysregulation used more strategies but had more negative affect" / "people who struggle most throw the most strategies at a problem and feel worse"
- **Abstract says:** "Higher event intensity and lower emotion dysregulation predicted greater strategy use during an emotional event. Additionally, greater event intensity and emotion dysregulation predicted greater daily negative affect."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that *lower* emotion dysregulation predicted using more strategies. The digest reverses this, and the entire pitch angle ("quantity versus quality — people who struggle most throw the most strategies at a problem") is built on the reversed finding. Pitched as written, this would be a factual error in print.
- **Suggested fix:** "people with *less* emotion dysregulation used more strategies per event, while greater dysregulation predicted more daily negative affect" — and rebuild the pitch angle around the fact that better regulators, not worse ones, deploy more strategies at once.

**Issue B. "Combinations" mislabels the effective strategies** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "We rarely use one coping strategy at a time — and only two combinations actually lower distress" / "only situation selection (removing yourself) and reinterpretation predicted lower daily negative affect"
- **Abstract says:** "Within instances of polyregulation, greater use of situation selection and reinterpretation predicted lower daily negative affect."
- **Problem:** These are two individual strategies whose use within polyregulation episodes predicted lower negative affect — not two strategy combinations. The headline's first clause ("We rarely use one strategy at a time") is also not quantified anywhere in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "When people stack coping strategies, only two of them predict lower distress"

---

### Study 19: Sensory sensitivity, not IQ, predicts whether self-injury in autistic children gets better or worse
**PMID:** 42657937 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline's "not IQ" contradicts the abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Sensory sensitivity, not IQ, predicts whether self-injury in autistic children gets better or worse"
- **Abstract says:** "Longitudinally, improvement in sensory features (p = 0.026) and higher T3 IQ (p = 0.039) significantly raised odds of decreasing SIB severity."
- **Problem:** Higher later IQ was a significant predictor of improvement alongside sensory features. The headline sets up a contrast the data do not support (the only IQ-related null is that baseline DQ did not predict worsening, and that DQ/IQ group differences emerged only at T3). The digest body reports the IQ finding correctly, so the headline contradicts the entry.
- **Suggested fix:** "Easing sensory sensitivities — and a higher IQ later on — predict whether self-injury in autistic children improves"

**Issue B. "Nearly all these preschoolers" stretches the prevalence figures** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Lead with the prevalence figure — nearly all these preschoolers showed some self-injury at some point"
- **Abstract says:** "At T1, 74% of the sample were characterized as having mild, moderate, or severe SIB… only 9% did not have SIBs at either timepoint."
- **Problem:** The 91% figure applies to the 122 children assessed at both timepoints, not to the full preschool sample, where 74% had SIB at T1. The digest body handles this correctly; the pitch line rounds it up.
- **Suggested fix:** "Lead with the prevalence figure — three-quarters of these preschoolers showed some self-injury at the first assessment, and among those followed to school age only 9% were free of it at both timepoints"

### Study 20: Sixteen hours of home audio reveals which mothers snap when a child gets very upset
**PMID:** 41642821 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Pitch asserts a null the abstract does not report** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "And the finding that 'how well you regulate emotions' in general does not predict how you respond to your own crying child."
- **Abstract says:** "These findings emerged after controlling for maternal difficulties with emotion regulation."
- **Problem:** Controlling for general emotion regulation difficulties is not the same as showing that general emotion regulation does not predict maternal responses. The abstract reports no test of that null. Unverifiable from abstract only, and it is the pitch's second hook.
- **Suggested fix:** "And the finding that a parenting-specific vulnerability predicted responses even after general emotion regulation difficulties were accounted for."

Sample (53 families, children 3–5), the 16-hour recordings, 4–10 coded episodes per child, LIWC emotion-word analysis, and the diathesis-stress interaction (increases in child negative intensity → more nonsupport and less positive emotion talk, only in high trait distress-reactivity mothers) are all accurate.

### Study 21: Virtual reality meditation shifts children's heart rhythms in four short sessions
**PMID:** 41484577 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract: N = 127, ages 9–12, four VR mindfulness sessions, increased high-frequency power and physiological coherence, improved emotional clarity and mood repair, greater HRV gains in Year 5 children, and the contested low-frequency interpretation flagged by the authors. The entry is appropriately explicit that the absence of a comparison group means novelty or expectation cannot be ruled out, and the NS fit of 5/10 is well calibrated to that.

### Study 22: Men in treatment for violence describe consent in a long-term relationship as something that stretches
**PMID:** 42647097 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Unprompted" and "after a certain number of years" are not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "these are men currently in treatment for intimate partner violence explaining, unprompted, why they think consent works differently after a certain number of years together"
- **Abstract says:** "To explore men's perceptions of sexual consent in intimate relationships, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 29 men… some viewed it as implied within committed relationships"
- **Problem:** Semi-structured interviews designed to explore consent are by definition prompted, and the abstract frames the "taken for granted" position in terms of commitment, not relationship duration.
- **Suggested fix:** "these are men currently in treatment for violence in intimate and family contexts explaining, in interviews about consent, why they think it works differently inside a committed relationship"

The three themes (fundamental, taken for granted, burden), the elasticity metaphor, N = 29, the treatment population and the University of Montréal authorship are all accurately reproduced, and the caveats correctly rule out generalization.
